content: Scopolamine, also known as hyoscine, has been used for decades to prevent and treat motion sickness, a condition characterized by symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, pallor, cold sweats, hypersalivation, hyperventilation, and headaches. Despite its widespread use, no systematic reviews had previously evaluated its effectiveness. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy of scopolamine compared to no treatment, placebo, other drugs, behavioral therapies, complementary therapies, or combinations of these approaches in preventing or treating motion sickness in individuals without known vestibular, visual, or central nervous system disorders. A comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), PubMed, EMBASE, and others, was conducted to identify relevant studies. The most recent search was performed on April 14, 2011. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared scopolamine to other interventions and evaluated outcomes such as the prevention or treatment of motion sickness symptoms, task performance, psychological measures, physiological changes, and adverse effects. Out of 35 potentially relevant studies, 14 studies involving a total of 1025 participants met the inclusion criteria. Scopolamine was administered in various forms, including transdermal patches, tablets, capsules, oral solutions, and intravenous formulations. Comparisons were made between scopolamine and placebo, calcium channel antagonists, antihistamines, methscopolamine, or combinations of scopolamine with ephedrine. The studies were generally small and varied in quality. Scopolamine was found to be more effective than placebo in preventing motion sickness symptoms. Comparisons with other agents were limited. Scopolamine appeared to be superior to methscopolamine and equivalent to antihistamines as a preventive treatment. However, evidence comparing scopolamine to cinnarizine or combinations of scopolamine and ephedrine was either minimal or inconclusive. Adverse effects were also evaluated. Scopolamine did not appear to cause more drowsiness, blurred vision, or dizziness compared to other agents. However, dry mouth was more commonly reported with scopolamine than with methscopolamine or cinnarizine. Importantly, no studies were identified that assessed the therapeutic effectiveness of scopolamine in treating established symptoms of motion sickness. In conclusion, scopolamine has been shown to be effective in preventing motion sickness when compared to placebo. However, there is insufficient evidence to draw conclusions about its comparative effectiveness against other agents, such as antihistamines or calcium channel antagonists. Furthermore, no randomized controlled trials have evaluated its efficacy in managing established symptoms of motion sickness.
